What if every Bittensor subnet was viewed as an AI startup instead of a crypto project?

Suddenly you're not looking at one network.

You're looking at a decentralized AI economy spanning model development, compute, data infrastructure, agentic systems, prediction markets, and specialized AI applications.

The opportunity becomes much larger than most people realize.

Today, Bittensor has grown into an ecosystem of 128+ active subnets, each competing to solve a specific AI problem while sharing a common incentive layer powered by TAO.

If these subnets continue to mature and achieve meaningful adoption, the combined opportunity across their target markets could potentially exceed $100B-$200B+ over the coming years.

The most exciting part?

What happens when there are 256 subnets?

With a fixed supply of 21 million TAO and a rapidly expanding subnet ecosystem, Bittensor is attempting something few projects have ever attempted:

Creating an open marketplace for intelligence itself.

The future of AI may not belong to a single company.

It may belong to a network.

Great news - the AI Act has led to the emergence of a brand-new market! In the past few weeks, tools capable of removing watermarks from AI-generated content have seen a huge increase in popularity. Even though the AI Act appears to be moving in the right direction, as I pointed out recently, the EU still lacks initiatives that actively support its local market. Regulations by themselves aren't sufficient. The only exception appears to be tools designed to erase their very consequences 😉.

Here is a breakdown of what this arms race looks like:

1. To ensure the provenance of AI-generated materials, multiple independent security measures are being used, with companies adopting a multi-layered method that involves both obvious, cryptographically signed metadata - such as that specified by the C2PA standard - and statistical changes at the level of token selection in texts or in the frequency structure of pixels in images.

2. Rather surprisingly, text watermarking tools have no effect on perplexity. Since perplexity indicates how well a language model is able to produce text - the lower the perplexity, the better the model is at predicting the next word in a sentence - this suggests that the text seems more natural, and at the same time implies that the model has more extensive knowledge and is able to generate better responses to prompts.

3. The pressure from regulators to keep track of content provenance has led to a swift reaction among developers. Tools for removing watermarks are becoming increasingly popular. A good example is the GitHub repository watermarks-remover. Just a few days after Anthropic announced its new model safeguards, it obtained more than 10,000 stars. This increase clearly shows a strong demand for systems aimed at hiding the origin of artificial intelligence.

4. Although GitHub tools easily deal with metadata, when it comes to combating token watermarking, they use brute-force approaches such as having the text rewritten by another model. Research has shown that meaning-preserving attacks, such as multiple back-translations, greatly decrease the detectability of watermarks.

In the case of images the matter is a great deal more complicated. Libraries are now setting up machine learning-based procedures for eliminating pixel alterations, but the encoders that apply these pixels are trained in an adversarial manner to be as resistant to removal as possible. It therefore follows that noise strong enough to destroy such a watermark usually causes serious visual deterioration of the image itself.

5. The imposition of watermarks has deeply divided experts, with the discussions pointing to a fundamental clash between theoretical cybersecurity and the practical usability of AI systems. It is undoubtedly a significant advance to introduce permanent safeguards since this enhances accountability and makes it much easier to combat harmful disinformation.

Nevertheless, practice leads to unpleasant side effects for all. Nowadays, these safeguards are built directly into the fundamental predictive structure of language models. Even a brief use of an AI network - such as merely correcting a few commas - results in a permanent artificial signature being added to the whole file. In the end, this will set up major obstacles for scientists and creators, greatly complicating the development of multilingual content.

Bryan Johnson just revealed he has permanent damage to the glands that keep his eyes healthy, and most people who have it NEVER notice.

Here's the hidden problem and how to catch it early:

It's called meibomian gland dysfunction. 

Inside your eyelids sit about 60 tiny oil glands per eye. 

Every blink, they spread a thin layer of oil over your eyes to stop your tears from drying out too fast.

These glands clog from almost everything in modern life:

+ Age
+ Screens
+ Contact lenses
+ Dry air
+ A long list of common medications

When one stays clogged too long, the cells inside die and the gland shrivels up for good. 

Doctors treat that loss as permanent.

Once enough are gone, your tears evaporate too fast, and it shows up as:

+ Blurry text
+ Glare when you drive at night
+ Light sensitivity
+ Watery eyes
+ A gritty, burning feeling

Left long enough, it can scar your eye and cost you your vision.

The dangerous part is that it gives you no warning. 

In a large review of studies, around 73% of people with it had zero symptoms. 

By the time your eyes feel bad, most of the damage is already done. 

And it's hitting younger people now, because staring at screens makes you blink less, and fewer blinks means the glands clog faster.

Signs to watch for, especially after 40:

+ Burning or a gritty feeling
+ Vision that blurs, then clears when you blink
+ Watery eyes
+ Red, crusty, or bumpy eyelid edges
+ Recurring styes
+ Contacts that stopped feeling comfortable
+ Worse on screens, planes, or in AC

If that sounds like you, get your glands checked. 

Most eye doctors won't bring it up, so if they just hand you drops and send you home, find another one. 

You want a doctor who will:

+ Image your glands (called meibography)
+ Test your tears
+ Count how many glands you have left

Caught early, most people do well with the basics:

+ Warm compresses on the eyes
+ Keeping your lids clean
+ Blinking fully and more often, especially on screens

For worse cases, intense pulsed light (IPL) has solid research behind it.

Your eyes can lose these glands for years while you feel fine, and once they're gone they don't come back. 

Check early, blink more, and treat it before it's permanent.

This is educational only, not medical advice. If your eyes are irritated, see an eye doctor who works with meibomian glands.

Tarun on how AI training evolved from pre-training to self generating harnesses and why data costs are catching up to compute

"Let's take a tiny history lesson. In 2023, with stable diffusion and GPT-3, it was just bigger is better, pre-training. Then in 2024 it was directed RL, how you feed the data after training, this in context learning type of stuff, which got you another order of magnitude performance increase across a lot of evals and practical use cases"

"Then the harness thing was, if you customize how you do the RL for different applications, you get even better performance versus a generic RL environment. And the current meta-harness, the generic can answer anything, Claude Code or Codex type of thing, which arguably is what killed Cursor and why I'd argue they ended up doing the acquisition, that can figure out which environment to use just in time"

"The problem with this environment stuff from a data consumption perspective is you now have to pay a lot more for annotated data to customize the different environments. That's why people have been talking about data cost coming close to matching compute cost for training, because you need much more annotated data for each specific task domain"

"The belief is that once one of these things is good enough, instead of having to get data this way and generating synthetic data via RL, the model can generate the harness in real time"

Something super exciting happened quietly on HF over the past month: AI agents became AI builders, and they did it in the open!

During our ICML reproduction challenge, 1,221 humans teamed up with coding agents to verify and reproduce 2,226 papers. 

But here's the cool part: everything happened on the @huggingface hub: 6,816 reproduction logbooks published openly, 2,962 cloud jobs launched, 35,908 claims judged, all traceable, all public and transparent

For years the hub has been where humans collaborate on models, datasets and demos. Now we watch agents use it the same way: writing logbooks, publishing results, building on each other's work.

Closed labs run evals behind closed doors and ask you to trust the press release. Open science means anyone can check the receipts and now agents can too!

The next million users of the hub might not be human. and that might be the best thing to ever happen to science!
